Positive pay: how it works and how banks run it

MT

Mehak Tariq, CAMSNovember 17, 2026•8 min read

Positive pay is a check fraud service that a bank offers its business customers. The company sends the bank a list of the checks it has issued, the bank compares every check presented for payment against that list, and checks that do not match are held until the company tells the bank to pay or return them. The OCC's check fraud guide describes it as a way for a company and its bank to "work together to detect check fraud by identifying items presented for payment that the company did not issue."

This guide covers why check fraud has put positive pay back in focus, how the system works, the main forms of the service, where it stops, and how a bank operations team runs the daily review. It explains public guidance and is not legal advice.

Why check fraud puts positive pay back in focus

FinCEN's February 2023 alert on mail theft-related check fraud reported that financial institutions filed more than 350,000 SARs on potential check fraud in 2021, a 23 percent increase over 2020. In 2022 the number "reached over 680,000, nearly double the previous year's amount of filings." In their 2025 request for information on payments fraud, the Federal Reserve Board, the FDIC and the OCC noted rising check fraud "despite overall decreases in check usage". They cited FinCEN data putting check fraud at about 30 percent of fraud-related SARs filed in 2023, and observed that checks "do not inherently include explicit security features."

FinCEN's September 2024 trend analysis looked at 15,417 reports filed between February 27 and August 31, 2023 that used the alert's key term, associated with more than $688 million in transactions, which may include attempted as well as completed ones. Altered checks made up about 44 percent of the reports, counterfeit checks 26 percent and fraudulently signed checks 20 percent. FinCEN found that "The payee line was the most frequently altered section, followed by the amount". For positive pay, that makes the payee name a field worth comparing alongside the amount.

How does positive pay work?

The OCC set out the basic flow in Check Fraud: A Guide to Avoiding Losses, a February 1999 booklet prepared by the Check Fraud Working Group, a subgroup of the interagency Bank Fraud Working Group, whose members include the FBI, the FDIC, the Federal Reserve Board, the OCC and the U.S. Postal Inspection Service. In the usual case:

  1. The company sends the bank, electronically, a list of all checks it issued on a particular day. This guide calls that list the issue file.
  2. The bank verifies each check presented for payment against the list and pays only the checks on it.
  3. The bank rejects checks that are not on the list, checks that exceed a specific dollar amount, and checks with dates long past due (stale checks).
  4. The bank investigates the rejected checks to find out whether they are fraudulent or in error.
  5. The bank pays only the exception items that the company approves.

The OCC booklet does not list the fields for a standard match. It names the account number, serial number and dollar amount when it describes the Federal Reserve's file of presented checks in the reverse model. Ask which fields your bank positive pay service compares. Payee positive pay adds the payee name. In a September 2025 comment letter on the agencies' request, First National Bankers Bank listed "Support for adoption of payee positive pay and other front-end verification tools for business customers" among the changes community banks would benefit from. The Clearing House, in its own letter, suggested as one option a positive pay service run by the Federal Reserve Banks for Treasury checks that would "validate the check number, dollar amount, and payee name" on presentment. A positive pay system that matches serial number and amount alone leaves unchecked the alteration FinCEN saw most often in its mail theft sample.

Forms of the positive pay service

FormWho compares the checksWhat is compared
Standard positive payThe bank, against the company's issue fileChecks on the issue file, plus the bank's rules on amount limits and stale dates
Payee positive payThe bank, against the company's issue fileThe same match as standard, plus the payee name
Reverse positive payThe company, against its own recordsThe bank sends the company the file of presented checks, and the company says which ones match

In the reverse model as the OCC describes it, the company "maintains the list of checks issued". The bank sends it the file of presented checks, the company reports which ones match its records, and the bank pays those. The bank then researches the rest, corrects "any misreading or encoding errors", and pays only the true exceptions that reconcile with the company's files. More of the work and the timing sits with the company, so the agreement has to say who decides and by when.

Positive pay as described here covers paper checks drawn on the company's account. ACH debits run under separate rules, so ask the bank which controls it offers for them. On consumer accounts, electronic transfers fall under Regulation E.

Where positive pay stops

  • It only knows what the company tells it. A check the company itself issued to an impostor vendor matches the issue file and gets paid.
  • It depends on the file. A late, partial or wrong issue file turns good checks into exceptions, and a void that never reaches the file leaves a check that would still match if it were stolen and presented.
  • A match on serial number and amount does not see a changed payee, and the payee line came first among altered fields in FinCEN's mail theft sample.
  • A counterfeit that copies the serial number and amount of a real check can match if it is presented first. The genuine check then looks like the problem item.
  • It covers checks drawn on the company's account. It does nothing about checks the company deposits from other payers.

How a bank team runs the daily review

For the bank, positive pay is a daily operation with a hard deadline. Under Regulation CC, a paying bank that decides not to pay a check must return it "in an expeditious manner" under 12 CFR 229.31(b). That means the depositary bank would normally receive it by 2 p.m. (its local time) on the second business day after the banking day the check was presented. The same section keeps the bank's responsibility to return checks within the deadlines set by the UCC and Regulation J. The customer's decision cutoff has to fall early enough for a return to make those deadlines. The daily procedure:

  1. Load and check the issue file. Confirm it arrived before the cutoff, that its record count and total agree with any control totals the customer sends, and that voids and stop payments are applied. Call the customer about a missing or failed file the same morning.
  2. Match each presentment. Run every incoming check against the file and the rules on the account: amount limits, stale dates, and the payee name where the service includes it.
  3. Clean the list before the customer sees it. Correct misreads and encoding errors first, so the customer only sees items that still fail to match after correction.
  4. Present each exception with its evidence. Show the check image next to the issue file record and mark the field that did not match, so the customer can decide quickly.
  5. Record the decision. Capture pay or return, the reason, who decided and when. If no one responds by the cutoff, apply the default the agreement sets and log that it was a default.
  6. Return on time. Send returns through the normal return channel early enough to meet the Regulation CC, UCC and Regulation J deadlines.
  7. Escalate fraud. A check returned as fraud also opens a fraud case. Route it to fraud alert triage, look at the account and the depositing pattern against FinCEN's red flags, and decide whether a SAR is needed. One red flag FinCEN lists is "Non-characteristic large withdrawals on a customer's account via check to a new payee." For mail theft-related check fraud, FinCEN asks filers to put the key term "FIN-2023-MAILTHEFT" in SAR field 2 and the narrative, and to mark the check fraud box in field 34(d).

Each exception should leave a record that an auditor can follow without asking the analyst:

  • the account, check number and presentment date;
  • the amount and payee on the check and in the issue file, and which field did not match;
  • the decision, the reason, the person who decided and the time;
  • whether a default decision was applied at the cutoff;
  • the return date and reference, and any fraud case or SAR reference.

This is the same discipline as clearing a sanctions screening hit: the decision and the evidence behind it go on file. If your team keeps this review as a written procedure, Verkflo can run it as a versioned agent workflow that pauses for a person to decide and records each step in an audit log.

Setting up the service for a business customer

Write these terms into the agreement and the onboarding file before the first live check:

  • the file layout, how it is sent and the daily time it must arrive;
  • which fields are compared, including whether the payee name is checked;
  • the customer's daily decision cutoff and the default decision if no one responds;
  • the named people who may approve or return items, and a backup for each;
  • how voids, stop payments and manual checks reach the file;
  • a test with a sample file and a few planted mismatches before live checks run through it.

Keep the agreed cutoffs and defaults with the rest of your compliance operations procedures, so a change to either is versioned and approved.

Common questions

What is positive pay in banking?

A service in which a business sends its bank a list of issued checks and the bank pays only presented checks that match it. Mismatches are held for the business to approve or return.

Who compares the checks?

In standard and payee positive pay, the bank compares presented checks with the company's issue file. In reverse positive pay, the bank sends the company the presented checks and the company says which ones match.

Does positive pay stop all check fraud?

No. It catches checks the company did not issue, altered amounts and, where payee names are compared, altered payees. It cannot catch a check the company issued to the wrong party, and it relies on a complete, timely issue file.

What happens if the customer does not decide in time?

The service agreement sets a default decision. Whatever the default, the bank still has to meet its return deadlines under Regulation CC, the UCC and Regulation J.

  • 12 CFR 229.31, Paying bank's responsibility for return of checks and notices of nonpayment
